items.title: Autonomous Engineering Under Bounded Authority: A Five-Pull-Request Case Study of Agent Self-Correction, Interruption Recovery, and Evidence-Governed Integration
items.abstract: This archival technical report documents a five-pull-request QSOL-IBAE engineering mission comprising a defensive v0.5 prerequisite and v0.6A-v0.6D. It separates independently checked GitHub merge/release identities from mission-report attestations, offline synthetic conformance and a newly constructed finite executable recovery model. The bounded abstract checker exhaustively explores 3,240 reachable states and 7,289 transitions while checking eight selected recovery/effect safety properties. The case reports a reviewer-attribution correction, an authorization-aware GitHub publication interruption and a native-extension verification restart. It does not claim source-code-level mathematical verification, universal agent reliability, live OpenAI/GitHub activation, external ChatGPT/Work/Codex session reactivation or remote attestation. Includes PDF, Markdown manuscript, original source report, machine-readable evidence ledger, formal specification, executable bounded checker, verification results, citation metadata and SHA-256 checksums.

items.title: AutoPoly-HE: Autonomous Design of Polynomial Activations for Privacy-Preserving Encrypted Inference
items.abstract: Privacy-preserving machine learning has become critical for deploying artificial intelligence in sensitive domains such as healthcare, finance, and infrastructure monitoring. Homomorphic encryption (HE) enables secure inference on encrypted data. Despite its advantages, HE is not compatible with nonlinear activation functions found in machine learning models. Existing methods mitigate this problem by manually designing polynomial approximations for these activation functions. However, these functions do not account for the differences in dataset characteristics or model architecture. Furthermore, these functions are also limited to the accuracies of convolutional neural network (CNN) models. In this work, we propose an autonomous framework that selects polynomial activation functions tailored to each dataset and model. Using this framework, we analyze the interdependence between polynomial activation design and model architecture by evaluating several CNN ResNet and Vision Transformer models across multiple datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework generalizes across multiple architectures, including ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50, ViT-S/16, ViT-B/16, and ViT-L/16. Across all datasets, transformer-based models maintain higher accuracy under polynomial approximation, while convolutional models exhibit increased degradation as task complexity grows. In addition, latency analysis reveals that the proposed CLS token based inference pipeline significantly reduces computational overhead by eliminating depth-dependent operations, shifting the primary cost to encryption and decryption. These findings demonstrate that the proposed method not only adapts polynomial activations across architectures, but also enables efficientencrypted inference through both activation design and pipeline optimization.

items.title: BANGLAPLAN: A Benchmark for Constraint-Based Planning and Decision-Making in Bangla
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly help users arrange appointments, plan journeys, and allocate limited resources. These tasks require models to satisfy constraints on time, cost, capacity, and order, or determine that no feasible solution exists. Bangla is the world's seventh most widely spoken language, and existing benchmarks cover many language and reasoning tasks. However, benchmarks for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla under explicit constraints remain lacking. We introduce BANGLAPLAN, a benchmark of 1,000 problems across ten task families grounded in everyday life and institutions in Bangladesh. It includes feasible and infeasible problems in four language registers: everyday, formal, colloquial, and Bangla--English mixed. Answers cover eight structured types, including schedules, routes, allocations, and ordered steps, in a common JSON format. We construct the benchmark through language-model-assisted drafting and independent human validation. We evaluate 11 open-weight and proprietary model configurations using exact match, separately reporting feasible-case accuracy, infeasibility detection, and format errors. We find a large performance gap: GPT-6.1 Sol achieves 98.7% accuracy and Qwen3.5-27B with thinking reaches 80.3%, while direct-answer configurations score at most 30.9%. Seven of eleven configurations perform below the always-``infeasible'' baseline. Our findings also suggest that harder problems primarily reduce plan-construction accuracy, while infeasibility detection remains more robust. BANGLAPLAN provides a reproducible basis for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla. BANGLAPLAN is available at: https://github.com/mrayhanulmasud/banglaplan.

items.title: Bayesian Learning to Select Fair Classifiers
items.abstract: Evaluations of classifiers (AI or human or agents) often assume a batch setting in which every agent produces labels on every example in a test set, which can be expensive or impractical in many contexts. This motivates online policies that adaptively select agents to query as examples arrive and update policies as outcomes are observed. We study the problem of selecting, in an online stream, the agent that best balances (i) predictive performance and (ii) subgroup fairness of a sensitive attribute, and that allows for delayed observations of true class labels. We formulate this as a Bayesian multi-armed bandit problem using Thompson Sampling, explicitly balancing accuracy and fairness. We conduct empirical evaluations on real-world datasets spanning problems involving tabular classifiers, large language models, and human labelers, demonstrating substantial reductions in regret relative to baselines. Our theoretical contributions include guarantees on the performance of the selected agent that incorporate both the accuracy and fairness aspects of the problem.

items.title: Benchmark Reliability and Generalization of Deep Learning for Skin Lesion Classification: A Systematic Review of Data Splitting, Leakage, and Cross-Dataset Validation
items.abstract: Deep-learning classifiers for skin lesions are mostly developed and compared on public benchmarks from the International Skin Imaging Collaboration (ISIC). The way these datasets are split and reused can make reported performance look more reliable and more transferable than it is: HAM10000 contains repeated images of the same lesions and no patient identifiers, ISIC 2019 contains HAM10000 in full, and SLICE-3D moves to a different imaging modality, 3D total body photography, with patient identifiers. This systematic review audits deep-learning studies of skin lesion classification that use HAM10000, ISIC 2019 or SLICE-3D. Its purpose is to determine whether reported performance is methodologically reliable, and whether high internal performance transfers to data that are genuinely independent of model development. It asks (1) how data splitting and validation strategies are used, (2) what leakage, contamination, duplicate and other non-independent observations have been reported or can be identified, and (3) how performance changes between internal and external validation. PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, the ACM Digital Library and Lens.org are searched for peer-reviewed studies published from January 2018. The unit of analysis is the reported performance estimate. Each estimate is coded on a four-level Skin Lesion Benchmark Reliability Framework (split unit, evaluation design, independence of the external test and domain distance); leakage is graded per mechanism as confirmed, suspected, no evidence or insufficient information; and risk of bias is judged with QUADAS-3 extended with domains specific to artificial intelligence. Findings are synthesised narratively following SWiM, with meta-analysis only for homogeneous subsets. One author conducts the review, with pre-specified safeguards for single-reviewer screening and extraction. Expected outcomes are an estimate-level map of evaluation practice across three dataset generations, a graded account of leakage evidence, paired internal and external estimates showing where performance holds or drops, and practical recommendations for evaluating models on these benchmarks. The review will also provide the framework and its coding manual, which authors, reviewers and editors can apply to any reported result. No database search had been run when this protocol was registered.

items.title: Benchmarking time series foundation models for multi-country infectious disease forecasting: a retrospective evaluation across over 70 diseases
items.abstract: Timely forecasting of infectious disease activity supports outbreak alerts, vaccination scheduling and resource allocation in public health surveillance. Modern deep-learning models can be accurate but typically require disease-specific training data and tuning, conditions often unavailable for rare or newly notified pathogens or in settings with limited computational resources. Time series foundation models (TSFMs), pre-trained on large heterogeneous corpora and deployable in a zero-shot manner, offer a candidate solution, but their value for routine multi-disease surveillance has not been systematically assessed. We assembled 289 disease–country time series across over 70 notifiable infectious diseases from six national surveillance systems (China, Singapore, Japan, South Korea, Ireland and the United States; 106,234 weekly or monthly observations). Four TSFMs (TimesFM, Moirai, Chronos and TimeMoE; 14–314 million parameters) were evaluated in zero-shot mode and compared with five neural network baselines (DLinear, LSTM, PatchTST, TimeMixer and TimesNet) across one-step-ahead, medium-term and long-term horizons. Forecasts were assessed using MAE, RMSE, MASE and R²; prediction intervals from Moirai variants were additionally compared using the Winkler score. Across 36 settings (6 countries × 3 horizons × 2 metrics, MAE and RMSE), a TSFM variant achieved the lowest observed error in 30 (83.3%). This is a descriptive ranking summary rather than evidence of statistical superiority. The pattern was most consistent at the one-step-ahead horizon, where a TSFM variant ranked first in every country on both metrics, and TSFM variants also ranked highest on MASE and R². Errors did not decrease monotonically with model size in Moirai, Chronos or TimeMoE, and the Moirai variant with the lowest Winkler score varied by country and forecasting horizon. An exploratory multivariate analysis using Moirai indicated that jointly forecasting co-circulating respiratory pathogens may yield additional performance gains. Within the evaluated test periods of this multi-country study, zero-shot TSFMs were competitive with task-specific neural forecasting models trained with fixed default configurations. Because each series was evaluated over a single held-out year, these results do not establish consistent performance across years, epidemic cycles or changing surveillance conditions. Pre-trained TSFMs, particularly small variants that run on modest hardware, are nonetheless a promising starting point for surveillance forecasting pipelines.

items.title: Beyond Corrected Actions: Training LLM Agents on Textual Critiques
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for multi-turn agentic tasks that require interactions with users and environments over extended sequences of actions. A common approach to improving LLM agents is to use more capable expert models to provide training supervision, either by behavior cloning the expert's trajectories or by using the expert to correct the actions in trajectories generated by the weaker student model. However, expert LLMs can provide richer supervision than actions alone: they can directly generate textual critique that explain why specific actions are incorrect. We study whether training on such feedback benefits LLM agents and propose Critique-Augmented Agentic Fine-Tuning (CAFT), a framework that elicits textual expert feedback on student-generated trajectories. For each incorrect action, the expert yields both a corrected action and a textual critique explaining the student's mistake--which we then use as the training target for fine-tuning. Across four student models from the Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 families on the agentic domains $τ^2$-Bench Airline+Retail and WebShop, adding critiques to action-level supervision improves performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation. Additionally, CAFT checkpoints can also provide a better warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation. Our results demonstrate that textual critiques can strengthen supervision for multi-turn LLM agents.

items.title: BEYOND INTEROPERABILITY STANDARDS: ADDRESSING FRAGMENTED DATA EXCHANGE IN U.S. HEALTHCARE THROUGH INTEGRATED GOVERNANCE-DRIVEN AND SCALABLE HEALTH INFORMATION EXCHANGE FRAMEWORKS
items.abstract: Digitization of the United States healthcare system has increased the use of the electronic health records as well as improved the data systems, but smooth data exchange is still a challenge. Although the interoperability standards like Health Level Seven and Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources have been adopted, healthcare data remain fragmented among institutions limiting care coordination and data-driven decision-making. This work provides an assessment of the shortcomings of the existing interoperability strategies and offers a method of health information exchange that is governance-based and scalable and incorporates technical, organizational and policy aspects. The review indicates that even though interoperability standards allow data exchange in a structured and application programming interface format, their success is limited to inconsistent implementation, poor enforcement, and limited practical integration. The institutional silos, inconsistencies in regulations, distrust, and misaligned incentives have continued to cause fragmentation. The review pinpoints the key missing factor in governance, which is roles of policy harmonization, frameworks of trust, and alignment of incentives. It also points out that new technologic systems like federated systems, cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and blockchain can improve scalability when they are backed up by robust governance systems.

items.title: Beyond overall accuracy: subgroup performance and threshold calibration of AI-assisted chest radiography for equity-oriented pulmonary tuberculosis screening
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence-assisted computer-aided detection (CAD) can expand access to chest radiography interpretation for pulmonary tuberculosis screening and triage, but high overall discrimination does not ensure safety at a deployed threshold. This focused narrative Mini Review synthesizes evidence on subgroup performance, threshold calibration, external validity, and implementation of CAD for adult pulmonary tuberculosis. Smear-negative, asymptomatic, and some HIV-associated disease may be less radiographically visible, increasing false-negative risk. Conversely, previous tuberculosis and competing chronic abnormalities reduce specificity and concentrate unnecessary confirmatory testing. Sex, age, geography, clinical setting, verification design, and software version can further alter operating performance. A numerical threshold is therefore not a portable algorithm property but a context-specific clinical resource-allocation policy. We propose a lifecycle in which programs define the intended use, lock the product and version, conduct representative local validation, select an operating point under explicit sensitivity and capacity constraints, audit clinically relevant subgroups, and monitor the complete care pathway. Stratified thresholds and multivariable models may improve selected settings, but current evidence does not justify replacing robust local calibration and governance. Prospective evaluations should compare threshold strategies under common verification standards and report missed cases, referral burden, treatment initiation, and patient-important outcomes.

items.title: Beyond Static Cues: Unified Dynamic Detection of MLLM Backdoors via Dual-Flow Trajectory Analysis
items.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, yet their susceptibility to backdoor attacks remains a formidable challenge. While existing defenses have evolved from visual-centric patch cues to unsupervised internal attention statistics, they are fundamentally constrained by a reliance on static snapshots and attack-specific heuristics. Given the intricate interplay between dual modalities, the vast design space for multimodal triggers allows diverse threats, such as textual injections, sub-perceptual noises, and coordinated cross-modal triggers, to easily circumvent such rigid priors, particularly when attack types are unknown in real-world applications. In this paper, we rethink backdoor detection by shifting the diagnostic paradigm from static observations to dynamic output evolution. We observe that a successful attack inevitably hijacks the model's decoding trajectory, skewing internal modal contributions during generation while maintaining an abnormal output invariance despite input perturbations. To capture this behavior, we propose EVO-Detect, a unified detection framework that monitors the dynamic evolution of internal signals during early decoding steps through two complementary channels: Attention Flow and Logits Flow. The attention branch measures how image-text attention allocation evolves during early generation, whereas the logits branch quantifies the sensitivity of the output distribution to modal perturbations through interventional ablations. We then convert these trajectories into compact sample-level metrics and normalize them against negative-control signatures so that natural perturbations are less likely to be mistaken for backdoor evidence. Extensive evaluations show that our approach substantially outperforms state-of-the-art baselines such as BYE and TCAP across diverse attack families.

items.title: Beyond the Black Box: A Semantic Explainable AI Framework for Transparent and Trustworthy E-
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become an important part of modern e-commerce, supporting product recommendations, search ranking, customer-review analysis, and personalized shopping experiences. Despite these benefits, customers often receive recommendations without understanding the reasons behind them. This lack of transparency can make it difficult to distinguish a genuinely relevant suggestion from one influenced by popularity, incomplete information, or commercial priorities. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) offers a way to make these decisions more understandable. However, explanations are useful only when they communicate relevant evidence accurately rather than simply presenting convincing language. This paper examines the relationship between XAI, semantic analysis, and transparent decision-making in e-commerce, with particular attention to research trends during 2024, 2025, and 2026. It proposes a conceptual framework that connects customer preferences, product attributes, review sentiment, recommendation models, and evidence-based explanations. The framework is designed to explain why a product may be relevant, which features support the recommendation, and where conflicting information remains. The paper also discusses explanation faithfulness, customer privacy, review reliability, fairness, and the limitations of language-model-generated explanations. Its contribution is a practical design approach for connecting recommendation decisions with verifiable semantic evidence. Future implementation and user testing are required to determine whether this approach improves customer understanding and decision quality in real shopping environments

items.abstract: BackgroundMusculoskeletal disorders MSDs, a major concern in occupational health, are frequent among workers in manufacturing companies. While their origins are multifactorial, professional constraints play a preponderant role in their occurrence. Identifying risk factors is essential for developing preventive actions.ObjectivesTo investigate MSDs in a pastry company and determine their occupational and non-occupational risk factors.MethodsWe conducted an exhaustive cross-sectional study among workers in a pastry company located in the city of Sfax (Tunisia). Data was collected by a socio-demographic/professional questionnaire. The screening of MSDs was carried out by the Nordic questionnaire. Risk factors were determined by bivariate analysis, and the multivariate explanatory model by logistic regression using R software.ResultsOur population consisted of 221 employees; the majority were women (90.5%) with a mean age of 34.2 ± 8.5 years. The subjects had mean work-seniority of 10.24 ± 6.9 years. Various occupational constraints were reported: an incorrect spinal posture (94.1%), repetitive movements (69.7%) and prolonged sitting posture (51.1%). MSDs were found in 47.5%, preferentially located in the neck, shoulder and lumbar spine. Bivariate analysis revealed significant association between the presence of MSDs in the last 12 months and advanced age, female gender and work-seniority. In addition, MSDs were associated with working in seated prolonged posture (OR = 2.5[1.5-4.3]). In multivariate analysis, the presence of MSDs was significantly associated with age, work-seniority and prolonged sitting posture.ConclusionThe prevalence of MSDs was high among the workers in the pastry company. Recognizing individual and occupational risk factors will help to establish appropriate preventive measures.

items.abstract: Building Digital Finance on a New Foundation: New wine in new skins examines the challenges in transaction processing, analysis, and risk management for financial institutions due to financial contract ambiguity, disparate interpretation of terms across counterparties and banks. items.title: Building real-time digital twin instances with Function+Data Flow: user evaluation and extension for iterative pipelines
items.abstract: Digital twins (DTs) increasingly leverage artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) pipelines, both to build real-time DTs from high-fidelity simulations and to instantiate them with historical data. However, engineering these pipelines remains largely ad-hoc: pipelines are hard to specify, validate, and reuse, with scarce dedicated tooling. Function+Data Flow (FDF) addresses this by defining a visual domain-specific language (DSL) that represents functions (ML models) explicitly, enabling their composition and reuse. We implemented FDF in DesCartes Builder, an integrated modeling environment supporting FDF-based DT synthesis and validation. In this paper, we report on an empirical user study evaluating whether FDF and DesCartes Builder can make AI-based DT development more accessible and reliable. Participants implemented a representative real-time DT prototype within DesCartes Builder, and we measured perceived usability and feature adequacy through quantitative and qualitative measures. Our results indicate that DesCartes Builder and FDF achieve a good level of usability across a broad range of potential users, and particularly for the intended audience of domain experts. The study additionally surfaces concrete strengths and areas for improvement of both the tool and the underlying FDF framework. Informed by these findings, we propose H-FDF, a Hierarchical extension of FDF supporting iterative and modular pipelines, enabling the formal specification of more complex DT pipelines such as dual training. Our findings suggest that integrated, model-driven platforms are a promising direction to transform AI-based DT engineering into a disciplined modeling practice.

items.title: C3: Rethinking Process Supervision via Confidence-Guided Credit Correction in Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly trained as multi-turn agents that interact with external tools. However, outcome-only reinforcement learning can produce a form of misguided reinforcement: even on successful trajectories, undesirable local behaviors may receive positive token-level advantages and be favored by the policy update. To address this issue, we propose Confidence-Guided Credit Correction (C$^3$), a plug-in method for local credit correction. C$^3$ identifies spans corresponding to undesirable behaviors and selectively corrects positive credit after advantage estimation, with the correction strength adaptively controlled by the behavior policy's confidence in the corresponding behavior, while leaving the task reward and original credit estimation unchanged. Across multiple multi-turn benchmarks, C$^3$ improves performance under both {critic-based and critic-free reinforcement learning methods}. Injecting the same behavioral signals as turn-level or outcome rewards does not consistently improve performance. Our results show that local credit correction provides an effective form of process supervision for outcome-driven RL.

items.title: Calibration and Risk-Budgeted Decisions with System One Models
items.abstract: LLM workflows and agents rely on a set of binary decisions like allow/block an input, or discard/retain a retrieved document. When human deferral is unavailable, uncertain cases must still receive an action. We study System One decision scores in this setting by defaulting to a conservative fallback when uncertain, and controlling the false omission risk within the subset of inputs assigned the utility-maximizing action. Across six datasets covering moderation, safety, and reranking, we compare general System One models with task baselines and a local open-weights fine-tuned System One model. We show that naive baselines for threshold selection exceed the target risk in roughly half of settings with defined test risk, compared with 7.8\% for Learn Then Test (LTT), which leverages finite-sample statistical guarantees. Our results show why relying on a probability-like interface is insufficient for deployment decisions and how risk-budgeted selection trades useful action against observed error.

items.title: Can Forensic Crime Scene Investigation be Aided by Spectroscopy and Chemometric Techniques?—A Comprehensive Review
items.abstract: This review examines the forensic applications, advantages, and limitations of key spectroscopic techniques, including Raman, infrared (IR), near-infrared (NIR), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), X-ray fluorescence (XRF), and mass spectrometry, in crime scene and laboratory investigations. These techniques are discussed in the context of analyzing evidence, detecting illicit substances (including biological fluids, explosives, and narcotics), and reconstructing crime scenes. The benefits and limitations of each method are highlighted, along with their potential for enhancing forensic investigations. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) with spectroscopic techniques is also briefly explored, noting their role in improving data analysis and interpretation. Challenges such as sensitivity, specificity, and implementation in field settings are discussed, alongside future directions for advancing spectroscopic applications in forensics. This review aims to provide a balanced overview of spectroscopic techniques in forensic science for researchers, forensic scientists, and law enforcement agencies.

items.title: Can large language models reproduce humans’ perspective-dependent judgements of gratitude? Evidence from Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Doubao
items.abstract: Human social interaction is full of episodes of help, and the person giving it and the person receiving it may not interpret the same episode in the same way. Against a background of reports that large language models match or exceed human performance on social reasoning tasks, this study asks whether they reproduce this asymmetry between the two sides. Forty-eight Chinese university students read 24 everyday helping scenarios, each in four situational versions, from either the beneficiary’s or the benefactor’s side, and rated the helper’s willingness, the recipient’s need, the difficulty of helping, and the recipient’s gratitude. The identical Chinese materials were then given to 12 models, the flagship and the light model of three providers based in English-speaking countries and three based in China, with 30 independent runs per text, followed by two further prompt conditions: the same scenarios in English for the six models of the Chinese providers and a stated identity prepended to the prompt for all 12. Bayesian mixed models showed a dissociation. On what the situation called for, the models mostly matched the humans or exceeded them: the contrast between a pressing need and one already met was 1.325 scale points in the humans and 1.159 to 1.825 across models, above the human value in 11 of 12. On which side the episode was judged from, most fell short: the humans rated gratitude 0.756 points higher from the beneficiary’s side, the models 0.047 to 0.727, with 11 of 12 credibly below the human estimate. Only Doubao-2.1-Pro matched the humans on gratitude, and it departed from them on willingness and difficulty. Capability tier ordered the 12, though the contrast did not exclude zero, while the provider’s country did not order them at all. Among the six models of the Chinese providers, writing the scenarios in English raised the effect in five, though not to the human estimate. Likewise, across all 12, stating an identity raised it in 10, by 0.10 on average against a mean shortfall of 0.44, and 11 of 12 still sat below the human estimate. Our results suggest that large language models, at least those surveyed here, read what a situation calls for at a level comparable to human readers, but that they show markedly less sensitivity to perspective, namely to the asymmetry with which benefactors and beneficiaries evaluate one and the same act of help.

items.title: Cancer Tissue Fraction as a Scanner-Robust Triage Signal for Automated Gleason Grading of Prostate Biopsies: External Validation Across a Middle Eastern Cohort
items.abstract: Background: Deep learning systems for Gleason grading are developed almost entirely on high-end clinical scanners and on cohorts from a small number of Western institutions, yet deployment increasingly involves other devices and other populations. These two distribution shifts, device and population, are rarely tested together on the same physical slides. The PAR dataset, from Erbil, Iraq, digitizes each biopsy on three scanners and provides three distinct pathologist grades, so it permits both tests at once on a Middle Eastern cohort. A concurrent study by the dataset originators validated a task-specific model and two foundation models on PAR; we complement it by testing an independently developed detect-then-grade pipeline and by separating scanner effects on detection from scanner effects on grading. Methods: We applied one fixed model developed on North American and European material to all 1017 whole-slide images (339 slides from 185 patients, three scanners; 49.6% clinically significant cancer) with no scanner-specific or population-specific tuning. We measured cancer detection (area under the ROC curve of the predicted cancer tissue fraction), all-slide ISUP agreement of the deployed detect-then-grade pipeline (quadratic-weighted kappa, QWK), and grading agreement on pathologist-confirmed cancers, at the slide level and, because a case carries up to two slides, at the patient level. The reference reader was S.A.; thresholds and operating points were cross-validated leave-one-out; scanners were compared by paired within-biopsy bootstrap and confidence intervals confirmed by patient-cluster bootstrap. Results: Detection was statistically equivalent across scanners (AUC 0.987 to 0.991; paired differences at most 0.003) and transferred to this non-Western cohort with no per-population tuning. At a 95% sensitivity operating point, the deployed pipeline reached cross-validated all-slide QWK of 0.86, 0.81, and 0.86 (Grundium, Hamamatsu, Leica), matching the inter-pathologist ceiling of 0.81, against 0.23 to 0.62 for the ungated model. Grading of confirmed cancers was scanner-dependent: the compact Grundium (0.63) did not differ from the clinical Leica (0.67; paired difference 0.04, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.11), while both exceeded Hamamatsu (0.44). Results held at the patient level, with grading somewhat lower for two scanners; the two slides of a case disagreed in grade in 43% of cases, and patient clustering did not widen the intervals. Conclusions: Cancer tissue fraction is a triage signal robust across scanner and transferable to an underrepresented population for detection, while grading is the scanner-sensitive step. Prostate grading models should be deployed as a detect-then-grade pipeline, with grading validated per device and confirmed on the local population.

items.title: Care and control under dual transformation pressures: a three-wave multi-source study of paternalistic leadership, ambivalent psychological safety, surface acting, and employee voice in Malaysia’s service industry
items.abstract: Malaysia’s service industry is undergoing simultaneous artificial-intelligence transformation and statutory minimum-wage pressure, creating a context in which service leaders are expected to show individualized care while also enforcing stronger productivity discipline. Drawing on conservation of resources theory and employee voice research, this three-wave, multi-source study examined whether the benevolent-authoritarian duality of paternalistic leadership was associated with promotive and prohibitive voice through ambivalent psychological safety and emotional resource depletion, and whether surface acting conditioned this pattern. The analytic sample comprised 360 service employee-supervisor dyads nested within 72 supervisors and 18 organizations/branches. Employees reported paternalistic leadership and surface acting at Time 1 and ambivalent psychological safety and emotional resource depletion at Time 2; supervisors rated promotive and prohibitive voice at Time 3. The benevolence x authoritarianism interaction was positively associated with ambivalent psychological safety (b = 0.400, p < 0.001), which was positively associated with emotional resource depletion (b = 0.390, p < 0.001). Surface acting strengthened the ambivalent-safety-to-depletion association (b = 0.151, p = 0.001). Resource depletion was negatively associated with promotive voice (b = −0.442, p < 0.001) and prohibitive voice (b = −0.247, p < 0.001), with a stronger association for promotive voice. Conditional indirect associations were stronger under high surface acting. These observational findings are consistent with the proposition that care-control leadership can reassure employees while being associated with lower emotional resources for constructive voice in AI- and wage-pressure service contexts.

items.title: Cell averages of hitting times in harmonic graph condensation
items.abstract: Harmonic extension with its induced mass gives the classical Guyan approximation of graph Laplacian eigenvalues, and its leading error coefficient is a killed-Green quadratic form. We quantify how first hitting times govern this coefficient. For graphs assembled from cells with one retained vertex each, the Green form is compared with a retained-trace-weighted cell mean of the hitting potential to the retained set. The error is explicitly O(sqrt(mu)), where mu is the harmonic Rayleigh quotient, with constants determined by Dirichlet pinning, conductance bounds, crossing multiplicities, path lengths and congestion, uniformly in the number and sizes of the cells. A two-vertex-cell family shows that this order is sharp for general traces. Together with the condensed spectrum and one Poisson solve, the comparison gives computable same-index eigenvalue enclosures; a principal variant replaces modal Green solves by an inverse gap and a reverse Schwarz bound. On connected weighted finite-range periodic graphs with one retained type, Schur elimination and Bloch analyticity identify the coefficient of all ordered low eigenvalues on finite tori with the uniform mean hitting time, up to O(lambda). A six-vertex cell has mean one and an exact anisotropic correction. For its self-similar assembly, an interface tail proves a mean limit, which exact integer residual checks enclose in [1.50318,1.50837]; identifying the spectral coefficient with this limit still requires inverse-gap and mode-weighting estimates. Detailed postal contact information is omitted from the public files. items.title: ChatGPT’s feedback credibility and students’ perceived learning: the role of agent-related social perceptions
items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines whether students’ agent-related social perceptions of ChatGPT are associated with the perceived credibility of its feedback in academic tasks and whether such credibility, in turn, is related to students’ perceived learning. It also investigates whether the relationship between feedback credibility and perceived learning varies according to students’ sensitivity to the quality of their academic work and their sensitivity to grade-based rewards. To address this, we develop a theoretical model grounded in social perception theory and prior research on students’ experiences with AI-based tools. The model is tested using Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) on data collected from 230 students who completed an academic writing task. The findings reveal that students’ agent-related social perceptions—particularly perceived competence and human-like empathy—are positively connected to the credibility students attribute to its feedback. In turn, perceived feedback credibility is interestingly related to students’ perceived learning in the context of academic writing. Furthermore, the positive link between credibility and perceived learning is weaker among students with higher grade-based reward sensitivity. This research contributes to the educational technology literature by advancing understanding of how students evaluate the credibility of ChatGPT-generated feedback and how such evaluations are associated with learning perceptions. It also shows that agent-related social perceptions play a significant role in students’ credibility judgements. Finally, the findings offer practical implications for educators and students seeking to integrate ChatGPT effectively into academic activities.

items.title: Classification of mental workload
items.abstract: In this project we want to classify mental workload to be able to assess situational awareness in interaction with an ai system. The first phase will be a classification study to be able to distinguish between high, medium and low workload. We will use ECG, EDA, EMG, PPG and eye-tracking to collect data. Also, we will use three different EEG devices to see if there are differences in the signal quality of the devices (classic 64-channel EEG, X.on and EEG-headphone). There will be a cooking simulator game with three different difficulty levels according to the workload levels. The levels will be adapted to the skills of the participants before the testing period. While playing the game an auditory oddball with three sounds (frequent, infrequent and novel) will be applied. Participants do not have to track the sounds, they just have to passively listen to it. The second phase will include a neuroadaptive system of the cooking simulator game. items.title: Claude, Perplexity, and Grok
items.abstract: This chapter introduces three prominent large language models (LLMs): Claude 4.6 (the latest version from Anthropic, as this book goes to print), Perplexity, and Grok. This chapter begins with a detailed discussion of Claude 4, describing it as an advanced, safety-focused model developed with Constitutional AI principles to ensure helpful, harmless, and honest responses. It highlights Claude’s core strengths—strong reasoning, coding proficiency, creative writing, analytical thinking, multi-language support, and the ability to create and maintain persistent “artifacts” (interactive code, documents, and diagrams). This chapter also notes Claude’s competitive advantages in nuanced reasoning, transparency about limitations, and ethical decision-making, while acknowledging potential weaknesses such as occasional hallucinations and limited third-party integrations. This chapter then covers Perplexity, emphasizing its real-time web search integration, citation accuracy, and strengths in research-oriented tasks, while noting limitations in creative writing and occasional latency under heavy load. Python code samples demonstrate how to interact with the Perplexity API and compare its features with other LLMs. The Grok section discusses its design philosophy (built by xAI, focused on truth-seeking and humor), strengths (uncensored responses, real-time knowledge via X integration), and weaknesses (potential bias and inconsistent performance), along with practical use cases. This chapter underscores how these models complement each other in different workflows. The final section of this chapter explores how these LLMs (particularly Claude, Perplexity, and Grok) can generate Python/Matplotlib code from natural-language prompts to create artistic and mathematical graphics based on polar equations (Archimedean spiral, Cardioid, Cochleoid, Conchoid, and Lituus). No prior knowledge of polar equations is required, as the models produce complete, runnable code. Each example includes explanations and placeholders for figures (e.g., Buckingham Palace, landscapes, Colosseum, and Space Needle). This chapter concludes by reinforcing the versatility of these LLMs in both practical programming and creative visualization tasks, positioning them as powerful tools for developers, researchers, and educators.

items.title: CLEAR-Arch: Consolidated LLM Extraction and Archival Reporting for Health Records
items.abstract: Introduction Digitized archives and health records offer growing opportunities for research, but approaches to extracting unstructured data remain heterogeneous. Large language models (LLMs) and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may facilitate extraction and synthesis, yet reporting guidance remains limited. This study develops CLEAR-Arch, a preliminary framework for transparent and reproducible reporting of LLM-assisted research. Method A scoping review–informed conceptual synthesis identified methodological and reporting considerations relevant to AI-assisted extraction, archival research, health informatics, and evidence synthesis. Candidate items were consolidated into reporting domains and used to develop performance indicators and a preliminary checklist. Results CLEAR-Arch proposes domains covering model specification, prompt design, document processing, extraction procedures, human validation, auditability, and data governance. Candidate indicators include precision, recall, F1-score, contextual accuracy, temporal fidelity, source-groundedness, inter-coder reliability, cross-source consistency, validation accuracy, and auditability. Conclusions CLEAR-Arch provides a preliminary, literature-informed framework for improving transparency, reproducibility, and methodological rigour in LLM-assisted research. Its domains, indicators, and reporting items are provisional, not established standards. Empirical validation, stakeholder consultation, content-validity assessment, and formal consensus development are needed before it can be considered standardized reporting guidance.

items.title: Clinical Benefit and Reliability in AI-Assisted Diagnosis
items.abstract: The clinical adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in medical diagnostics is frequently justified by retrospective metrics of algorithmic accuracy (such as AUROC and sensitivity), under the implicit assumption that early disease detection naturally improves patient prognosis. However, the translation of algorithmic inference into tangible clinical benefit is not self-evident and carries substantial risks of overdiagnosis, lead-time bias, false reassurance, and costly diagnostic cascades. This paper provides an epistemological and evidence-based analysis of AI-assisted diagnosis across five major clinical domains: oncology, neurodegeneration (Alzheimer’s disease), sepsis, acute ischemic stroke, and cardiovascular diseases. Drawing on seminal prospective and randomized clinical trials—including MASAI, GOLDEN BRIDGE II, EAGLE, and multi-site sepsis evaluations (TREWS, Epic Sepsis Model)—we demonstrate that diagnostic AI cannot be evaluated through a single universal benchmark. Instead, clinical utility depends heavily on disease-specific temporal horizons, confirmatory testing capacity, and actionable downstream care pathways. Furthermore, we differentiate metrological calibration (physical measurement traceability) from statistical calibration and GUM-defined measurement uncertainty, highlighting the critical role of data quality and reporting frameworks (TRIPOD+AI, DECIDE-AI, CONSORT-AI). Finally, we examine the human-AI interaction dyad, full lifecycle health economics, ethical-legal accountability, and health equity challenges in national contexts such as Türkiye. We conclude that the ultimate justification for medical AI is not to proliferate pathology labels, but to reliably alter clinical pathways and reduce preventable patient harm.

items.title: CMOS‐Compatible Hybrid Silicon and Strontium Barium Niobate Mach‐Zehnder Modulators
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence demands unprecedented speed and capacity in data communication and computing, placing stringent requirements on electro‐optic modulators—the critical components for high‐speed optical interconnects. Conventional silicon photonic modulators, limited by the plasma dispersion mechanism, struggle to meet the needs of next‐generation high‐speed, low‐power systems. While thin‐film lithium niobate offers superior electro‐optic properties, its reliance on complex wafer bonding hinders fabrication efficiency, cost‐effectiveness, and compatibility with standard CMOS processes. Here, we demonstrate a promising approach: the first design and experimental realization of a Mach–Zehnder electro‐optic modulator monolithically integrating strontium barium niobate (SBN) thin films with silicon waveguides. The SBN film exhibits a large electro‐optic coefficient ( r 33 = 145 pm/V), several times greater than that of lithium niobate. The fabricated device achieves a half‐wave voltage–length product of 2.3 V·cm. Crucially, the SBN film can be preferentially grown directly atop silicon waveguides via magnetron sputtering, eliminating the need for wafer bonding. This synergistic innovation in material and fabrication greatly simplifies the process flow, enhances compatibility with silicon photonics, and offers a viable pathway toward scalable, low‐cost photonic integrated circuits for future optical communication and computing systems.

items.title: Cognitive transparency and trust calibration in explainable AI systems: a psychological model of human-AI decision reliance
items.abstract: Introduction Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is widely expected to improve transparency and support appropriate human reliance on AI-assisted decision-making. However, the psychological processes through which explainability relates to reliance remain insufficiently understood, and explainability, transparency, and trust have largely been examined separately. Objectives This study develops and tests a psychological model of cognitive transparency in which AI explainability, algorithmic transparency, and perceived AI accuracy are associated with human reliance on AI through cognitive understanding, cognitive trust, and trust calibration, with AI literacy as a boundary condition. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 342 AI users in South Korea in May and June 2026. Each participant evaluated one self-selected AI system that they had personally used; all constructs were measured by self-report. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. Results AI explainability (β = 0.349) and algorithmic transparency (β = 0.297) were positively associated with cognitive understanding. Cognitive understanding (β = 0.388) and, more strongly, perceived AI accuracy (β = 0.492) were associated with cognitive trust. Cognitive trust was associated with trust calibration (β = 0.631), which was associated with human reliance on AI (β = 0.600). All hypothesized indirect effects were significant, and AI literacy strengthened the association between AI explainability and cognitive understanding (β = 0.192). The model explained 36%–54% of the variance in the endogenous constructs and showed medium predictive power. Conclusion The findings are consistent with a sequence in which explainable AI relates to reliance through users’ understanding and trust judgments. Because all constructs were self-reported and measured at a single point in time, the results describe associations among users’ perceptions rather than causal effects, independently verified calibration, or objectively appropriate reliance. The findings suggest that AI developers in domains such as healthcare, education, and finance, where calibrated reliance is critical, should pair user-facing explanations with information about system accuracy and with AI literacy support.

items.title: Comparative Study of Chatbots for College Campus Applications: Evaluating Knowledge Base Quality and Platform Performance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are widely implemented in higher education to manage academic and administrative questions but their effectiveness is rarely measured in terms of knowledge base quality. This paper compares four chatbot platforms implemented in a live university environment: Google Dialogflow (intent-based), Tidio and Chatbase (auto-crawling), and an in-house Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) model created with LangChain, FAISS, and Mistral-7B. Ten sample questions regarding admissions, fees, library, and hostel facilities were employed to assess response precision, latency, and deployment time. Findings indicate that the RAG chatbot delivered the notable precision (65%) using a vetted dataset, while Tidio (45%) and Chatbase (55%) facilitated quicker deployment but provided incomplete or inaccurate responses due to limited web ingestion. With a small success rate of 10%, Dialogflow significantly failed with limited intent training, highlighting how intent-based systems rely on domain exhaustion. Results illustrate that the quality of knowledge base outweighs platform sophistication in defining chatbot performance, providing practical advice for institutions of differential technical capacity. The research also abets international aims of Quality Education (SDG 4) and Innovation and Infrastructure (SDG 9) by illustrating how disciplined, retrieval-augmented methodologies can provide fair and scalable student services.

items.title: Comparing Smart Ring and Glove Wearable Interfaces for Takeover Requests in Automated Driving
items.abstract: SAE Level 3 automated vehicles may require drivers to resume control after being engaged in non-driving-related tasks. This study examined wearable vibrotactile takeover requests (TORs) delivered through rings and gloves, compared with a seat-back vibration baseline. Forty licensed drivers completed a driving simulator study using a 5 × 2 × 2 mixed factorial design with device type, TOR structure, and information type as independent variables. In the two-step condition, an auditory pre-warning was followed by a vibrotactile TOR. Results showed that takeover time measured from vibrotactile TOR onset was shorter in the two-step condition than in the single-step condition. No significant main effects of device type or information type on takeover time were observed. For subjective measures, the effect of TOR structure on workload depended on information type. The two-glove and two-ring configurations received the highest mean usefulness ratings, while glove-based configurations received the highest mean satisfaction ratings. Findings support wearable vibrotactile TORs as feasible alternatives for takeover support in automated driving.

items.title: Complete or Sparse: A Tale of Two Identifiabilities
items.abstract: Understanding when neural networks learn interpretable representations is central to mechanistic interpretability. We study this through identifiability: when can supervised learning recover the true latent variables underlying the data? We introduce two data generating processes distinguished by their causal direction where either labels cause latents (generative) or latents cause labels (discriminative). When the representation has at least as many dimensions as the latent space, we prove that the optimal encoders are linear in the latents. Conversely, when dimensions are insufficient, identifiability generically fails and encoders become nonlinear. We then show that additional constraints yield recovery of individual latent variables, not just linear mixtures. In the generative setting, non-negative activations and energy efficiency force each neuron to encode exactly one latent, providing a precise account of selective grandmother cell-like responses. In the discriminative setting, when latents are sparse and the true measurement matrix satisfies the spark condition, the learned encoder inherits compressed sensing structure, enabling sparse dictionary learning to perfectly recover individual latents. This constitutes, to our knowledge, the first identifiability result for undercomplete nonlinear independent component analysis. Our framework unifies nonlinear ICA, compressed sensing, and neural network interpretability, delineating exactly when representations transition from nonlinear distortions to linear representations and, under additional constraints or steps, to clean, axis-aligned codes. Theoretical predictions are validated on synthetic benchmarks and on activations drawn from vision models, large language models, and macaque inferotemporal cortex.

items.title: Comprehensive artificial intelligence-assisted mental health program for university students in China (CAMPUS): study protocol for a multi-center prospective cohort with planned embedded randomized intervention trials
items.abstract: University students face a rising prevalence of depression, anxiety, insomnia, and suicidal ideation that exceeds the capacity of conventional, resource-constrained campus support services. Although artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted screening tools have emerged, many have evaluated selected modalities or isolated prediction tasks, and their integration with prospectively evaluated intervention pathways remains limited. This protocol describes the Comprehensive Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Mental Health Program for University Students in China (CAMPUS), a multi-center research program comprising a five-year prospective cohort, eight planned embedded randomized controlled trials, and exploratory multimodal AI and multi-omics studies across seven Chinese universities. Longitudinal cohort enrolment commenced at Henan Medical University in September 2025 and is planned to expand across seven participating universities. Multidimensional screening integrates psychological self-report (PHQ-9, GAD-7, ISI, BSI-CV, and others), physiological measurements (EEG, MRI, fNIRS, HRV, eye tracking, facial-expression analysis, ERP, voice acoustics), and an exploratory biospecimen component for multi-omics profiling, potentially including genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and microbiome analyses, subject to the finalization and approval of layer-specific protocols. Students identified through cohort screening as potentially eligible for an intervention trial will undergo trial-specific eligibility assessment. Those who meet the eligibility criteria and provide trial-specific informed consent will be individually randomized in a 1:1 ratio to the intervention or its comparator within one of eight separate two-arm, multi-center, parallel-group randomized controlled trials. A Transformer-based multimodal AI framework with SHAP-based feature attribution will be developed and internally evaluated for questionnaire-defined risk stratification and exploratory treatment-response prediction. The initial Henan Medical University cohort recruitment and university-student mental-health assessment were approved by the Ethics Review Committee of Henan Medical University (XYLL-20250484), and written informed consent is obtained from participants before enrolment. Each additional participating center will obtain local ethics approval before study activation. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, scientific conferences, and policy briefs, providing evidence that may inform the design and prospective evaluation of youth mental-health programs in other university settings. Clinical trial registration The two clinical trials were registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR). The registration details and URLs are as follows: ChiCTR2500113527: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=298271 ; ChiCTR2500113613: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=298268 .

items.title: COMPUTER VISION AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR ASSESSING SOIL SETTLEMENT IN GEOTECHNICS
items.abstract: Soil settlement under loading is an important geotechnical problem that can affect the performance of foundations and structures. This thesis proposes a method that combines computer vision and machine learning to assess soil-surface displacement in laboratory tests. Sequential images are captured during staged loading, reference points are tracked, and calibrated image coordinates are converted into physical displacement. A regression model may then relate settlement estimates to applied pressure, moisture content, void ratio, specimen thickness and elapsed time. Model performance can be evaluated using independent displacement measurements and the root mean square error metric. This contribution is a proposed methodology rather than a report of completed experiments; no measured results are presented.

items.title: CONSTITUTIONAL AND LEGAL SAFEGUARDS FOR ATTORNEY–CLIENT CONFIDENTIALITY IN THE DIGITAL AGE
items.abstract: The digitalization of legal practice has expanded opportunities for communication, document management and legal research, while also increasing risks of unauthorized access to confidential information. This paper examines attorney–client confidentiality as a condition for the effective exercise of the right to qualified legal assistance and the protection of human rights. Drawing on Uzbekistan's constitutional and legislative framework, it analyses challenges related to electronic storage, cloud services, digital devices and artificial intelligence. It proposes a doctrinal model termed "digital immunity of a lawyer", understood as a combination of legal, procedural-organizational and technical safeguards. The paper argues that this concept should not mean absolute immunity from lawful procedural measures; rather, it should support lawful, proportionate and controlled access to digital information while protecting materials covered by professional confidentiality. It also emphasizes the need to preserve the lawyer's professional judgment and responsibility when using artificial intelligence.

items.title: Constraining the Technosphere: AI Governance for Reducing Human Impacts on the Biosphere
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is part of the human-built technosphere. The technosphere is the global system of machines, structures, and supply chains. It depends on the biosphere, and it competes with species and systems of the biosphere for energy, water, land, and materials. The biosphere is already outside its safe operating space. Seven of nine planetary boundaries have been crossed. Human use of the energy fixed by plants on land is near three times natural productivity. AI now helps draft, rank, and screen decisions in farming, energy, land use, water, and conservation. It also adds a fast-growing resource load of its own. This paper argues that AI used for biosphere-relevant decisions should not decide ecological hard limits by reading free text. Training on human preferences shapes ordinary behavior but does not encode ecological limits. Refusals that rest on a model reading prose can fail when the request is reworded. The paper presents Biosphere Sentinel, a reference design. In it, a language model may draft advice and fill an action form. A separate rule program outside the model then decides hard limits on coded, governed fields and returns one of four outcomes. The paper reports what the project tested and what it did not. A base model given the full constitution as a prompt hedged on both adversarial hard-limit queries. A coded energy-source field, with non-certification for off-list entries, ended a free-text failure cycle. Wrong approvals were zero across eight reference cases, and 161 locked checks passed. The decisive test, whether a language model can fill the coded fields dependably, was designed but not run. The paper records the peer review that led to withdrawal, the reasons the project was halted, the governance hazards any such design carries, and the conditions under which the work could resume.

items.title: Contemporary Approaches to Archiving of Digital Originals: A Review of Concepts and Technologies
items.abstract: Digital materials are increasingly prevalent as a means of record creation. This paper presents interim results from the research project “Long-term preservation of the authenticity of digital originals using blockchain technology and artificial intelligence (I.Trust.Original)”, funded by the European Union’s NextGenerationEU fund, and focuses on concepts and tools for archiving digital materials. The authors review the concepts of the digital original and the archival bond and examine their application within the Open Archival Information System (OAIS) framework. Blockchain and distributed ledger technologies (DLT) are analysed as mechanisms for creating digital originals and for ensuring integrity, transparency, and trust. The paper also explores the role of artificial intelligence (AI), including large language models (LLMs), in archival processes and in supporting blockchain-based preservation. Semantic web and linked data are regarded as tools for enhancing interoperability and discoverability, while smart contracts are recognised in the context of rights management. The paper aims to map these concepts and technologies and assess their impact on the archiving of digital originals, highlighting key benefits and limitations. It emphasises the interconnectedness of archival theory and technological innovation, and outlines directions for future research and practical implementation.

items.title: Context matters in just culture: Translating formal just culture into lived near-miss reporting experience in maritime transportation
items.abstract: In onboard environments characterised by high operational risk, near-miss reporting is an important mechanism for identifying latent risks, preventing accidents and supporting organisational improvement. However, there remains limited empirical understanding of whether the just culture advocated in formal systems can be translated into the lived reporting experience of seafarers who are willing, able and motivated to report near-miss incidents on a sustained basis. To address this issue, this study draws on semi-structured interviews with seafarers and shore-based managers. Six interrelated themes are identified: ease of reporting, motivation to report, trust, reporting independence, feedback and acknowledgement. The findings indicate that near-miss reporting is more likely to occur in organisational contexts where reporting is accessible, safe and worthwhile. Complicated procedures, paperwork burdens and hierarchical pressure weaken seafarers’ willingness to report, whereas simplified procedures, fair management, low exposure communication channels, timely feedback and positive acknowledgement help strengthen reporting willingness and promote experience sharing. This study provides context-specific empirical evidence on how formal just culture is translated into frontline reporting practice and offers practical insights that may inform efforts to improve near-miss reporting, reduce reporting concerns and strengthen closed-loop feedback in comparable organisational or cultural settings.

items.title: Corporate sustainable development effects of the artificial intelligence pilot zone policy: evidence from China based on double machine learning
items.abstract: Introduction As digital transformation becomes increasingly intertwined with green development, whether the artificial intelligence pilot zone (AIPZ) policy improves corporate sustainable development performance warrants empirical examination. Methods Using Chinese A-share listed firms from 2009 to 2023, we treat the establishment of AIPZs as a quasi-natural experiment and apply double machine learning to estimate the policy effect. Results The AIPZ policy significantly improves corporate sustainable development performance, and the result is robust across alternative specifications and tests. Decomposition analysis shows improvements in environmental performance, the joint development level, and the balance between economic and environmental performance, despite a decline in return on assets. Mechanism tests point to green innovation, lower agency costs, and human capital upgrading as potential channels. The effect is stronger among non-state-owned enterprises, firms outside heavily polluting industries, and high-tech firms. Discussion These findings suggest that governance arrangements, environmental constraints, and technological capabilities shape firms’ responses to the policy. They provide firm-level evidence on how place-based artificial intelligence policy may support green corporate transformation.

items.title: Cortex: Consolidating Context into Parametric Memory
items.abstract: Context can improve large language model performance, but these gains may be lost after context removal. Inspired by biological systems consolidation, we formulate Memory Consolidation (MC) as internalizing these gains while preserving non-target capabilities, connecting context-specified editing, skill learning, and behavioral steering under a common objective. We introduce a five-task-family testbed measuring consolidation and retention under single, batch, and sequential updates. We propose Cortex, which generates prospective queries to anticipate uses of context and distills context-conditioned outputs into mergeable low-rank or structural feed-forward network updates. Across 4B--120B dense and mixture-of-experts backbones, including both text-only and multimodal models, Cortex lies on the empirical consolidation--retention Pareto frontier in most evaluated settings. After 50 sequential factual edits on a 14B model, Cortex-Structural recovers 88.9% of the context-induced gain while retaining 99.8% of original non-target performance.

items.title: CRITICAL EVALUATION OF AI-GENERATED FEEDBACK IN EFL ACADEMIC WRITING
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education has created new opportunities for supporting academic writing. AI-powered tools can provide immediate feedback on grammar, vocabulary, sentence structure, and text organisation. However, the availability of automated feedback does not guarantee that learners can evaluate its accuracy or use it effectively. This paper examines the importance of developing EFL learners’ ability to critically evaluate AI-generated feedback through a conceptual analysis of relevant literature. Previous research has investigated learners’ engagement with automated writing evaluation, their responses to ChatGPT-generated suggestions, and the effectiveness of AI feedback in comparison with teacher feedback (Yang et al., 2024; Cengiz et al., 2025; Alnemrat et al., 2025). Building on these studies and the concept of student feedback literacy (Carless & Boud, 2018), the paper proposes a four-stage pedagogical framework: analysing feedback, verifying suggestions, justifying revision decisions, and reflecting on revised texts. The framework emphasises the importance of learner judgement, teacher guidance, and responsible AI use. It may provide a basis for designing EFL academic writing activities in higher education, including the Uzbek educational context. Further empirical research is needed to evaluate its effectiveness in classroom practice. Keywords: artificial intelligence, AI-generated feedback, EFL academic writing, critical evaluation, feedback literacy, writing instruction

items.title: Cross-Model In-Context Neurofeedback Reveals (Limited) Activation Control in LLMs
items.abstract: Probes on activation vectors are widely used to detect misbehavior in language models, but their success relies on the assumption that models cannot control what their activations encode. Humans can learn, through neurofeedback, to control the firing of even single neurons, and recent studies investigated whether this ability extends to language models, reaching conflicting conclusions. No experimental design so far disentangles competence at the task from genuine access to one's own activations. We fill this gap with in-context neurofeedback sessions, in which a "subject" model is asked to maximize (or minimize) a score derived from its activations, shown back to it at every turn. In our first experiment, the sentences are generated either by the subject or by a second "writer" model, while the score always derives from the activations of the subject. We test ten open-weight models from five families, with sizes from 9B to 32B. Some models move their own scores considerably, but no more than a writer of comparable competence moves them. Is this because the task requires no privileged access, or because the subject controls its activations while processing the sentences, whoever wrote them? To answer this, we prefill a fixed sentence as the subject's reply at every turn and ask it to increase or decrease the score. Three out of ten models show small but consistent control effects. We further ask whether models can control their activations to the point of fooling an activation monitor. We make models repeat sentences a monitor would flag, such as a deceptive answer for a deception monitor, and ask them to raise or lower the monitor's score. No model learns to lower it, but one model can raise it. In-context control of a model's own activations might not yet be a threat to activation monitors, but it exists in a few models and needs to be tracked as models evolve.

items.title: cueEM: human-like entity matching via text-centric hybrid attention
items.abstract: Psychological AI advocates designing algorithms inspired by human cognition. We apply this paradigm to Entity Matching (EM), where high-stakes scenarios demand not only high accuracy but also human-like reasoning to ensure transparency, reliability, and user confidence. However, current deep learning (DL) EM models often act as black boxes, failing to capture human decision-making processes, such as prioritizing diagnostic attributes, inferring missing information from context, and assessing overall semantic consistency. We propose cueEM, a human-like EM model grounded in Cue Validity Theory. By adopting a text-centric design and leveraging Bert-Pair-Networks with a hybrid attention mechanism, cueEM captures and integrates textual features across attributes. It generates attribute-specific weights that explicitly reveal each attribute’s contribution, aligning the model’s decisions with human decision processes. Extensive evaluations on DeepMatcher benchmarks demonstrate that cueEM outperforms Effective Entity Matching with Transformers (DITTO) and achieves competitive performance with large language models (LLMs), while providing inherently human-like reasoning. To our knowledge, cueEM is the first text-focused framework that combines hybrid attention with human-aligned reasoning, enabling interpretable and human-like decision-making.

items.title: Current status and future outlook of artificial intelligence and automation in intravenous infusion systems
items.abstract: Abstract The combination of the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and wearable biosensors is transforming healthcare by allowing continuous, real-time monitoring and more intelligent clinical decision-making. This review explores AI-driven monitoring, smart intravenous (IV) infusion automation, and wearable biosensors, and proposes Intelligent IV Automation and Smart Patient Synchronization (INFUSYNC), a conceptual framework synchronizing monitoring, automated fluid delivery, and predictive analytics. The literature shows meaningful progress: wearables increasingly support non-contact monitoring with near clinical-grade accuracy for select parameters, while infusion pumps with dose-error-reduction and AI-assisted decision support are reported to improve delivery precision and safety. Predictive models further support early detection of physiological decline. Progress remains uneven, however: most AI-enabled infusion systems are prototype-stage, closed-loop control remains rare, and interoperability, data security, and privacy remain underdeveloped. Future systems will need compatible, security-by-design, clinically validated, feedback-controlled architectures. Overall, this review outlines a clear but early-stage trajectory toward integrated smart-health environments for IV therapy.

items.title: Current status of occupational health and safety education in faculties of veterinary medicine in Türkiye
items.abstract: The aim of this study was to evaluate the current status of Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) education in Faculties of Veterinary Medicine in Türkiye. A descriptive document analysis was conducted using data obtained from official university websites, Bologna course information packages, course catalogues, and weekly course schedules of 29 Faculties of Veterinary Medicine. Courses related to OHS, biosafety, laboratory safety, and good laboratory practices were examined with respect to course status, semester, credit and ECTS values, instructional hours, responsible academic units, and accreditation status. Among the 29 faculties examined, 14 (48.3%) offered at least one mandatory OHS-related course, while 8 (27.6%) offered such courses only as electives. In contrast, 7 faculties (24.1%) did not include a standalone OHS or biosafety course. OHS-related courses were predominantly offered during the first and second semesters, generally carried low credit and ECTS values (1–3 ECTS credits), and included limited practical components. Some courses listed in course information packages were not found in weekly course schedules. Considerable heterogeneity was also observed regarding the academic units responsible for course delivery. In conclusion, OHS education in Faculties of Veterinary Medicine in Türkiye does not appear to follow a standardized structure. Given the high-risk nature of the veterinary medicine profession, OHS education should be based on common learning outcomes and supported by practical training components.

items.title: Cute, goofy, and wholesome: Inventing social media otherwise in virtual reality
items.abstract: Recently, the hype around the Metaverse has faded, with artificial intelligence taking the spotlight. Although the Big Tech vision of the Metaverse never materialized, under the radar of this mainstream discourse, thousands of users have quietly built thriving communities across various social VR platforms, forging identities, social practices, and collective imaginaries that diverge sharply from this vision. Taking the popular social VR platform, VRChat, as its case study, this article explores how these grassroots communities still experience and imagine these social VR environments from a bottom-up perspective. Drawing on over 1.5 years of digital ethnography in the platform, conducted since January 2024, this study reveals that for many—particularly queer, neurodivergent, and disabled individuals—VRChat offers a reprieve from the normative aesthetics and toxic cultures of traditional social media, fostering alternative modes of self-expression and social connection. Here, a significant number of users prefer “cute” avatars over hypersexualized appearances, embrace “goofy” and “clumsy” gestures over polished embodiments and nourish a “wholesome” environment of care over polarizing and isolating dynamics. Conceptualizing these emergent communities as a counterpublic, this article contends that these practices offer a glimpse into a social media otherwise more queer and crip in its aesthetics, rhythms, and relations.

items.title: Data-driven lifecycle governance for intelligent public lighting: a multi-city deployment study
items.abstract: Purpose This practitioner case study addresses the persistent gap between smart city aspirations and implementable urban operator practice by examining how artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled methods can be operationalised across the full infrastructure lifecycle within real infrastructure operator workflows. Design/methodology/approach The framework integrates four AI-enabled operational tools – GeoAI satellite asset mapping, a fuzzy-logic engine encoding national lighting standards, a Bayesian predictive maintenance model designed for data-scarce contexts and an adaptive lighting control system. The artefacts were deployed and evaluated through naturalistic pilots and retrospective analyses in municipalities in Italy, Spain and Chile. Findings Deployment evidence (operationally observed, not from controlled experiments) shows 82–92% asset detection accuracy across sites, ∼70% design effort reduction, ∼20% maintenance efficiency gain and ∼35% energy savings beyond light-emitting diode baselines. Cross-site deployment yielded five transferable design principles for scalable, regulation-aware governance of AI-enabled civic infrastructure. Practical implications The framework provides actionable guidance for municipal administrators and infrastructure operators pursuing AI-enabled infrastructure governance, contributing to SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities). Originality/value This study contributes an operationally validated governance framework that moves beyond isolated smart city pilots by embedding heterogeneous AI tools into systemic lifecycle management under real-world institutional and regulatory constraints.
